introduction-remote-is-not-zoom-from-hom.core: Remote work is a communication architecture, not a location. Copying office habits onto video calls produces meeting overload across time zones. Async-first design (written, documented, discoverable) makes distributed work effective.

first_principles.problem: A 'remote' company runs back-to-back Zoom calls, so people in other time zones are excluded or work at midnight.
truths: Time zones make real-time coordination expensive.
derivation: Default to **async**; use sync for high-bandwidth needs.
Keep a **handbook-first** single source of truth.
**Shift communication left**: decide in writing.
Make **writing** the core skill; use **RFCs/ADRs** for decisions.

analogy.title: A relay team across time zones
analogy.story: Each runner hands off a clear baton (a written update) instead of waiting for everyone to run together.
analogy.breaks: Some things (conflict, brainstorming, bonding) benefit from synchronous time, so use it intentionally.

example.title: Office habits vs async design
flow: Office copy: 8 daily calls, APAC excluded
Async: written status, decisions in docs, 1 weekly sync

check.q: Why does copying office habits fail for remote teams?
check.a: Synchronous meetings require overlapping time, excluding other time zones and fragmenting focus.

handbook-first-culture-the-gitlab-model.core: GitLab's handbook-first approach documents how the company works (processes, decisions, values) in a public, versioned handbook. Changes are made by merge request, and answers live in the handbook rather than in people's heads or chat history.

first_principles.problem: Knowledge lives in Slack threads and senior people's memory, so new hires constantly interrupt others and decisions get re-made.
truths: Versioned docs show the history of decisions.
A single source of truth reduces duplication.
derivation: **Document first**, then share links.
**Change the handbook** via MRs (reviewed and versioned).
**Answer questions with links**; if no link exists, write it.
Keep it **organised and searchable**.

analogy.title: A company's operating manual as a living wiki
analogy.story: Everyone can read and improve the manual, so it's always current.
analogy.breaks: Handbooks go stale without ownership and the habit of updating them.

example.title: Answering a process question
flow: Q in Slack: 'How do I request a new repo?'
If missing → write page, then link

check.q: What's the core habit of a handbook-first culture?
check.a: Documenting first and answering questions by linking to the handbook, writing the page if it doesn't exist.

managing-time-zones-the-shift-left-of-co.core: Across time zones, design processes that don't need real-time agreement: written proposals with comment periods, clear handoff notes, explicit owners and deadlines, and small overlapping windows reserved for what truly needs sync.

first_principles.problem: Decisions wait 24 hours for each round of back-and-forth because questions are vague and only answered in overlap hours.
truths: Each async round trip can cost a day.
derivation: Write **complete messages**: context, question, options, deadline.
Use **comment periods** for decisions.
Write **handoff notes** at the end of each day.
Protect **overlap hours** for true sync needs.

analogy.title: Sending a letter vs. a phone call
analogy.story: A letter has to contain everything the reader needs, because they can't ask a quick question back.
analogy.breaks: Urgent incidents still need synchronous paging and follow-the-sun on-call.

example.title: A vague vs a complete async message

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A decision in one round trip.

code.text:
✗ "Thoughts on the DB thing?"
✓ "Context: orders DB at 85% CPU. Options: (A) read replica, (B) cache layer.
I recommend A (details: link). Need decision by Thu 17:00 UTC; I'll proceed with A if no objections."

example.outcome: time zones become a feature, not a blocker.

check.q: Why include a deadline and default action in async messages?
check.a: It avoids stalls across time zones by allowing progress if nobody objects in time.

writing-is-the-primary-skill.core: In remote organisations, writing is how you influence, decide and execute. Clear, concise, well-structured writing (BLUF, headings, explicit asks) is a core engineering skill, not a soft one.

first_principles.problem: Engineers who explain well in person seem ineffective remotely because their messages are long, vague or unstructured.
derivation: Put the **bottom line up front**.
Use **structure**: headings, bullets for scanning, tables.
Make an **explicit ask**: what you need, from whom, by when.
**Edit** for brevity; know your **audience**.

analogy.title: A newspaper article
analogy.story: The headline and first paragraph tell the whole story; details follow for those who want them.
analogy.breaks: Over-structured writing can feel robotic, so stay human and warm.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Readers get it in 10 seconds and act.

code.text:
**TL;DR:** Migration 80% done; on track for Friday. Need DBA review of step 4 by Wed.
**Done:** services A–D migrated
**Next:** E, F (Thu)
**Risk:** step 4 schema lock — @dba-team please review PR #812

check.q: What does BLUF mean in written communication?
check.a: Bottom Line Up Front: state the key point or ask first.

the-rfc-and-adr-structured-async-decisio.core: RFCs collect structured feedback on proposals asynchronously before decisions. ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) record what was decided, why and with what consequences, so distributed teams can decide without meetings and remember why.

first_principles.problem: Remote teams struggle to make design decisions, and six months later nobody knows why a choice was made.
derivation: **RFC**: problem, proposal, alternatives, open questions, deadline for comments.
**Decide** with an explicit owner.
**ADR**: context, decision, status, consequences (short).
Store ADRs **with the code**.

analogy.title: Meeting minutes for decisions, without the meeting
analogy.story: Proposals circulate, comments are collected, and the final decision is filed for posterity.
analogy.breaks: Process overhead for small decisions is wasteful, so use ADRs only for significant ones.

code.text:
# ADR-014: Use Postgres for order service
Status: Accepted (2024-05-02)
Context: Need relational integrity; team expertise in Postgres.
Decision: Aurora Postgres, single-writer.
Consequences: Multi-region writes not supported; revisit if expanding to APAC.

check.q: What's the difference between an RFC and an ADR?
check.a: An RFC proposes and gathers feedback before a decision; an ADR concisely records the decision made and its rationale.
